concepts.title: Protein Data Types and Their Uses

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Protein Data Types and Their Uses' refers to.
questions.a: Protein informatics feeds on every raw form a protein can take - micrographs of heat-denatured aggregates, solutions for physico-chemical study, MALDI sequence fragments, assembled sequences, PDB crystal files, interaction maps, NMR and mass spectra, and hypothetical proteins read straight out of genomes - each type answering a different question from marker design to drug-target mapping.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Protein Data Types and Their Uses'.
questions.a: Match the raw data type to the question: crystals reveal interactions, fragments rebuild full sequences, and genome reads reveal proteins never seen in a lab.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Protein Data Types and Their Uses' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Predicting Secondary and 3D Protein Structures' refers to.
questions.a: When no crystal exists, computation fills in: APSSP, CFSSP, SOPMA and GOR forecast helices and sheets; homology modelling on MODELLER or SWISS-MODEL copies a solved relative; threading forces the chain onto a known backbone for fold prediction; QUARK builds the model de novo from sequence alone, and InterPRO or CDD carves the chain into domains recorded later as PDB coordinates.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Predicting Secondary and 3D Protein Structures'.
questions.a: Close relatives give global folds by homology, distant hints give local folds by threading, and sequence alone still yields a de novo model.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Predicting Secondary and 3D Protein Structures' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Molecular Graphs and Substructure Searching' refers to.
questions.a: Chemicals live in computers as molecular graphs - atoms as nodes, bonds as edges - the same node-edge logic that later draws pathways like glycolysis; searching them often runs in two stages, a bitstring screen that discards obvious non-matches, then a subgraph isomorphism test that confirms every atom and bond of the query sits inside the candidate, and reaction searches add atom mapping from reactants to products.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Molecular Graphs and Substructure Searching'.
questions.a: Filter fast with bitstrings, confirm exactly with subgraph isomorphism, and map every atom to its product in reaction searches.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Molecular Graphs and Substructure Searching' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Pharmacophore Models of Ligand Recognition' refers to.
questions.a: A pharmacophore is not a molecule but the abstract set of steric and electronic features - charged groups, rings, hydrophobic patches - arranged in space that a ligand needs to wake a biological target; modelling these features explains how structurally unlike ligands can still dock the same receptor.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pharmacophore Models of Ligand Recognition'.
questions.a: Collect the features, not the atoms - a pharmacophore maps what must be present and where, not what the molecule is.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Pharmacophore Models of Ligand Recognition' taught, and from which source text?
